client: I've been struggling a lot since my mom passed away six months ago, and honestly I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help. It feels like everyone around me has just... moved on, like it's old news, but for me it still feels like it happened yesterday. I guess I came here because I don't know what else to do, but part of me wonders if therapy is really going to change anything.
therapist: I'm really glad you came, even with that doubt sitting alongside you — that took courage, and it makes complete sense to feel uncertain when the pain is still so raw and the world around you seems to have moved on without you. Grief doesn't follow a schedule, and feeling like it just happened yesterday, six months later, tells me how deeply you loved her. I'm not here to rush you or promise magic, but I am here to sit with you in this at whatever pace feels right — what do you think has been the hardest part to carry on your own these past months?

client: I think the hardest part is the silence at night, when there's no one to call or text anymore and I just sit there with my phone in my hand feeling completely stupid about it. She was the person I told everything to, and now all those thoughts just kind of pile up with nowhere to go. I didn't realize how much of my daily life was built around her until she was gone.
therapist: That image of sitting with your phone in your hand is so quietly heartbreaking, and there's nothing stupid about it at all — it's actually a beautiful sign of how real and central that connection was to your everyday life. What you're describing, that sudden absence of a person who held so much of your inner world, is one of the loneliest kinds of loss there is. I'm curious — when those thoughts start piling up at night with nowhere to go, what kinds of things are you finding yourself most wanting to tell her?

client: Honestly, it's kind of everything and nothing at the same time. Like, I'll see something dumb on TV and think "she would have hated that" and I just want to text her about it, or I'll have a hard day at work and she was always the one who could talk me down from spiraling. But then there's also this heavier stuff I never got to say, like whether I was actually a good enough friend to her, and that's the part that really keeps me up.
therapist: There's so much tenderness in those small moments — the dumb TV show, the hard work day — and it sounds like grief is woven into the ordinary fabric of your days in a way that's both sweet and painful at once. But I want to gently stay with that heavier thing you mentioned, because "was I a good enough friend to her" sounds like it carries a real weight that might be worth looking at together. What does that voice in your head actually say when it tells you that you weren't?

client: It says things like... "You were too busy, you kept canceling plans, and then suddenly there was no more time to make it right." It tells me I prioritized stupid, forgettable things over being there for her in the last few months, and that she probably felt like she wasn't important to me. And the worst part is I can't even argue back with it, because some of it is actually true — I did cancel on her, more than once.
therapist: That voice is being very loud and very one-sided right now — it's collecting every cancellation as evidence against you, but I notice it's not allowing in any of the other evidence, like the fact that you were the person she told everything to, or that your grief six months later is this deep and this present. Canceling plans is something almost every person does with the people they feel safest with, precisely because we trust those relationships to hold — it doesn't automatically mean she felt unimportant to you. If your mom were sitting here right now, what do you think she would say about whether you were a good friend to her?

client: I want to believe that, I really do. But when I try to imagine what she'd say, I just... I don't know if I can trust what comes up, because maybe I'm just telling myself what I want to hear to feel better. And honestly, part of me feels like even asking that question is a way of letting myself off the hook too easily.
therapist: There's something really honest and even admirable in what you just said — you're holding yourself to a high standard and refusing to take easy comfort, which speaks to how much integrity matters to you. But I want to gently offer another way to look at it: questioning whether you deserve forgiveness isn't the same as being rigorous about the truth, and sometimes that inner critic disguises itself as fairness when it's actually just being harsh. What would it look like to examine the evidence about the kind of friend you were — not to let yourself off the hook, but to actually get to the truth rather than just accepting the prosecution's case?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to accept it, but it also feels like maybe you're just trying to make me feel better rather than actually helping me see clearly. Like, what if the evidence really does point to me being a bad friend to Marcus? I skipped his dad's funeral because I told myself I was too anxious to handle it, and no reframe is going to change that that happened.
therapist: You're right that no reframe changes the fact that you didn't go, and I want to be clear — I'm not trying to talk you out of the truth or make you feel better at the expense of seeing clearly. But I notice you've shifted from talking about your mom to Marcus, and I wonder if that's worth pausing on — are these separate wounds, or is there a pattern you're seeing in yourself that feels bigger than any one moment? What I'm most interested in is understanding what was actually happening for you when you made that choice, not to excuse it, but because "I was too anxious" might be the beginning of the story rather than the whole thing.

client: I think you're right that it's not just about my mom or Marcus separately — there's something bigger there, like I keep finding myself on the outside of moments that matter, and then telling myself I couldn't help it. But when you ask what was actually happening when I made that choice, I feel this tightness in my chest, because honestly I think part of me was afraid that if I showed up, I'd still somehow feel alone in the room. It's easier to blame the anxiety than to admit I might have been protecting myself from something I couldn't name.
therapist: What you just said is genuinely profound, and it took real courage to name it — that the anxiety might have been protecting you from a deeper fear of being present and still feeling alone, which is a much more vulnerable thing to admit than just "I couldn't handle it." That pattern, of standing outside moments to avoid a pain that might happen anyway, makes so much sense as a way of surviving, even as it leaves you with regret afterward. I'm wondering — when you imagine actually being in those moments, fully present, what is it you're most afraid you'd feel?

client: I think what I'm most afraid of is that I'd be fully there, completely open, and still feel that hollow ache of being disconnected from everyone around me. Like, I'd do everything "right" — I'd be present, I'd try — and it still wouldn't be enough to feel like I actually belong. That almost feels worse than just avoiding it, because then I'd have no excuse left, no distance to hide behind.
therapist: What you're describing is one of the most painful fears a person can carry — that even your best, most open self might not be enough to feel truly connected, and that trying and still feeling alone would be harder to bear than never trying at all. That belief, "even if I do everything right I'll still end up disconnected," sounds like it might be something you've felt for a long time, maybe even before your mom died. I'm curious — where do you think that fear first came from, that belonging might just not be available to you?

client: Yeah, I think you're right that it goes back further than losing her. Even as a kid I remember feeling like I was kind of on the outside of things, like everyone else had been given some manual on how to connect and I just... didn't get one. I don't know if that's something that can actually be fixed, or if it's just who I am at this point.
therapist: That image of everyone else having a manual you never received is such a lonely way to have moved through the world, and I want to sit with how long you've been carrying that. But I also want to gently push back on the idea that this is simply "who you are" — because what you've done in this conversation today, the honesty, the self-reflection, the willingness to look at painful things without flinching, those are actually the exact skills that connection is built on. What do you think it would mean for your life if that sense of not belonging turned out to be a very old story you learned rather than an unchangeable truth about you?

client: That's... a hard question to sit with, honestly. Part of me wants to believe what you're saying, that it's just an old story, but another part of me keeps thinking, well, if I had those skills you're describing, wouldn't I have more people in my life by now? It feels less like a story and more like evidence that just keeps piling up.
therapist: That's such a fair challenge, and I don't want to brush past it — the loneliness in your life feels like real, concrete proof to you, not just a narrative. But I want to offer one gentle observation: the skills you have and the opportunities you've had to use them are two very different things, and someone who learned early that connection wasn't safe or available might actually become quite skilled at protecting themselves from the very thing they need most. What would it mean to consider that the "evidence" might be less about your capacity for connection and more about how long you've been, understandably, keeping yourself just out of reach?
